Saylor","date":"2026-09-30","url":"/media/articles/why-digital-credit-issuers-strengthen-one-another","thumbnail":{"url":"https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltf8d808d9b8cebd37/blt0978dfb251d1f143/whyDigitalCreditIssuers.jpeg"},"content":"<p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">A shared capital foundation. Three amplifiers. An industry worth building together.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>I want Strive to succeed. I want every well-managed issuer of Bitcoin-powered Digital Credit to succeed.</strong></p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Strategy and Strive are building businesses around the same financial foundation. BTC is Digital Capital. STRC and SATA are Digital Credit. MSTR and ASST are Digital Equity.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">We offer different securities, make independent decisions and serve investors with different objectives. We can compete for an individual investment while strengthening one another’s long-term opportunity.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The reason is fundamental: when responsible companies bring new investors, new capital and new capabilities into the Bitcoin economy, the benefits can extend across the industry. Our shared opportunity is much larger than any contest for an individual allocation.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>We are building an industry together.</strong></p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">The largest opportunity is outside our industry.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The world’s capital markets are enormous. <a href=\"https://www.sifma.org/research/statistics/fact-book\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">SIFMA reports</a> that global equity market capitalization reached $157.8 trillion and global fixed-income debt outstanding reached $160.7 trillion at the end of 2025. One tenth of one percent of either market is roughly $160 billion.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">That is the scale against which we should measure our opportunity. Bitcoin treasury equities and Bitcoin-powered credit are young categories seeking recognition within much larger markets.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Each part of our industry offers investors a different proposition:</p><ul style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Digital Capital competes for long-term capital allocations.</strong> Bitcoin seeks a place alongside equity indices, gold, real estate and other assets investors use to preserve and grow wealth. Vehicles such as SPY, QQQ and GLD represent familiar alternatives for those dollars.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Digital Credit competes for income allocations.</strong> STRC, SATA and other instruments must earn consideration alongside private credit, high-yield bonds, preferred securities, and bond or income ETFs.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Digital Equity competes for growth capital.</strong> MSTR, ASST and other Bitcoin treasury companies must demonstrate why their business models deserve a place alongside technology stocks and other growth-oriented equities.</li></ul><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">These investments have different structures and risks. What connects them is the competition for an investor’s attention, understanding and capital.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Every time an investor becomes comfortable making a first allocation to our industry, the opportunity expands. The greater challenge is convincing that investor to enter the category at all.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Bitcoin connects our balance sheets.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">People often interpret corporate competition through familiar pairs: Nike and Adidas, Coke and Pepsi, Target and Walmart. In a mature market, winning a customer often means taking a sale from another company. Price competition can compress margins.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Those businesses can also help their categories grow. But Bitcoin treasury companies have an additional economic connection: we hold the same underlying capital asset.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">A successful advertising campaign for one beverage company does not automatically increase the value of another beverage company’s assets. A rise in Bitcoin’s price increases the market value of the Bitcoin held by every treasury company, including companies that did not raise the new capital contributing to demand.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Our balance sheets are separate. Our liabilities, reserves, governance and financing terms differ. Yet the value of our core capital is linked through a common market.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">I think of the opportunity as a triple amplifier: appreciation of Digital Capital, adoption of Digital Credit, and recognition of Digital Equity. The shared Bitcoin foundation powers the first and most important driver.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">The first amplifier: appreciation of Digital Capital.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">When a company attracts new capital and uses it to acquire Bitcoin, it adds demand for an asset with a constrained supply. To the extent that broader adoption supports Bitcoin’s price, the benefit reaches other Bitcoin holders.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">A stronger Bitcoin price can increase the asset coverage behind existing claims, strengthen common equity and expand financing capacity. The magnitude depends on each company’s capital structure and obligations.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This is why a successful Bitcoin acquisition by Strive can be constructive for Strategy, and why a successful acquisition by Strategy can be constructive for Strive. Both companies are helping develop demand for the capital on which their businesses are built.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Individual purchases do not guarantee higher prices. Market prices reflect net demand across the world. The structural point is that our interests in the adoption and long-term value of Bitcoin are aligned.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>The value created by broader Bitcoin adoption can reach every balance sheet built on Bitcoin.</strong></p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">The second amplifier: adoption of Digital Credit.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">A new credit category must earn trust. Investors need to understand the asset base, the payment structure, the priority of their claim and the management decisions supporting it. Institutions need research, trading history, liquidity and a framework their investment committees can evaluate.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Several capable issuers can build that foundation faster than one issuer acting alone. Each well-designed product and each demonstrated record of financial discipline provides more evidence for investors to study.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">An investor who learns how to evaluate SATA is better prepared to evaluate STRC. An institution that develops a Digital Credit framework for STRC may find it easier to consider other issuers.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">As understanding, liquidity and confidence improve, investors may require a smaller premium for the category’s unfamiliarity. That can narrow credit spreads and reduce financing costs across qualified issuers.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">For Strategy, stronger demand could support additional STRC issuance on attractive terms and, where market conditions and the security’s terms permit, a lower dividend rate. Tighter spreads can improve financing economics even though changes in benchmark interest rates may offset the effect on the total yield investors require.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Lower financing costs can expand the set of transactions that create value for common shareholders. They can also give issuers greater capacity to maintain reserves and improve their products.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Bitcoin appreciation is uncertain and Bitcoin itself pays no coupon. The potential economic margin between long-term asset returns and financing costs must be earned through disciplined management. It is not a locked-in interest spread.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>A peer that helps investors understand Digital Credit can help lower the cost of capital for the industry.</strong></p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">The third amplifier: recognition of Digital Equity.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Investors are also learning how to value the companies creating these products.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Digital Equity combines exposure to Bitcoin with ownership in an operating financial business. At Strategy, MSTR offers Amplified Bitcoin and participation in the business we are building around Digital Credit: product development, capital formation, investor distribution and active balance sheet management.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">As more companies demonstrate that this model can operate through different market conditions, equity investors have more evidence with which to assess its durability and growth potential.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">That recognition can support broader ownership and higher valuations for companies that execute well. Multiples such as mNAV, which measures valuation relative to Bitcoin asset value, may expand when investors assign greater value to a company’s future ability to raise and deploy capital productively.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Stronger equity valuations can, in turn, create opportunities to issue common stock on terms that add value per share, acquire additional Bitcoin, strengthen liquidity or retire more expensive claims.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">A premium must be earned. More issuers do not automatically produce higher multiples, and growth must exceed the costs of dilution, financing and maintaining liquidity. But successful peers can help establish that Bitcoin treasury management is a durable business model deserving serious institutional analysis.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>Evidence that the model works can increase the opportunity for every company capable of executing it.</strong></p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">The amplifiers can reinforce one another.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">These three drivers are connected.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">A stronger Bitcoin capital base can support greater confidence in Digital Credit. Broader credit adoption can improve financing economics. Better economics and sustained execution can strengthen the Digital Equity proposition. Productive financing can then expand the capital base and the business built around it.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The potential benefits extend across asset values, financing margins, equity multiples and growth rates.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">They also extend beyond any single transaction. An additional credible issuer can help justify more analyst coverage, more institutional research, better trading infrastructure and more investment in distribution. A useful innovation can establish a higher standard for the next product.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Some of the most valuable work is creating awareness and legitimacy: helping investors understand what they own, demonstrating responsible capital allocation and building a record of performance through difficult markets.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>Every responsible issuer contributes to a body of evidence that the next investor can use.</strong></p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">More issuers make the industry more investable.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Many investors are willing to allocate to an asset class but unwilling or unable to concentrate that allocation in a single company. Their mandates may impose issuer limits. Their judgment may call for exposure to multiple management teams and capital structures.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">A market with only one issuer cannot fully satisfy that demand. Several credible issuers can.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This means a new entrant can unlock capital that would otherwise remain outside the category. Product diversity also allows investors to choose among different payment structures, seniority, currencies, durations, distribution channels and risk profiles.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Issuer diversification can reduce exposure to one company’s management, governance or financing decisions. It does not remove the common exposure to Bitcoin or the possibility of correlated losses.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Strategy cannot serve every investor with one security. Strive cannot either. A larger selection of well-designed products makes the whole industry more useful.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>More credible issuers can mean more capital available to the category.</strong></p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Complementarity is already visible.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">On March 11, 2026, <a href=\"https://investors.strive.com/news-events/news-releases/news-details/2026/Strive-Announces-SATA-Enhancements-and-Purchase-of-Bitcoin--STRC/default.aspx\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">Strive disclosed a $50 million purchase of STRC</a>.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">An issuer of Digital Credit can also be an investor in another issuer’s product. Each purchase has its own investment merits and risks, but the example illustrates how these businesses can become customers of one another while developing their own securities.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The same complementarity can extend to asset managers building diversified portfolios, distributors reaching new investors, and financial institutions developing additional products around Digital Credit.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>The opportunity grows as more independent businesses find useful ways to participate.</strong></p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Think Ford and Standard Oil.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The rise of the automobile offers a useful analogy. Ford and the oil industry, including Standard Oil and its successors, participated in an expanding system of complementary businesses. More cars created more demand for fuel. Better access to fuel and service made automobiles more useful.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Manufacturers, refiners, service stations, road builders and finance companies helped make one another’s businesses possible. Each company had its own economics, but the development of the wider system created opportunities across the industry.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">We are building a financial ecosystem with the same need for complementary capabilities.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Digital Capital provides the foundation. Digital Credit serves investors seeking income. Digital Equity finances and owns the businesses building these products. Digital Money supports payments and settlement. Digital Derivatives can help participants transfer and manage risk.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Together, these capabilities can make the Digital Assets industry more useful to households, businesses and institutions.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Strategy and Strive have a shared interest in helping that ecosystem grow. So do the other responsible companies developing its capital, products and infrastructure.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Build an industry worth investing in.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The shared foundation makes standards matter. A weak issuer can damage confidence across the category, just as a strong issuer can help build it. Falling Bitcoin prices, widening credit spreads and contracting equity multiples can also reinforce one another.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The positive-sum opportunity depends on responsible execution: sound capitalization, prudent liquidity, transparent disclosures, useful products and a commitment to creating value for investors.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">We can support public education, better market infrastructure and rules that allow responsible innovation. Each company will continue to set its own terms, make its own capital-allocation decisions and earn investors’ confidence through its own performance.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">That is a constructive form of competition. It improves products, expands access and can bring more capital into the entire industry.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">I welcome capable companies willing to do that work. Every responsible builder can help strengthen our shared capital foundation, broaden the acceptance of Digital Credit and demonstrate the potential of Digital Equity.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>When we build on Bitcoin, we have an interest in one another’s success.</strong></p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>Let’s build the industry together.</strong></p><h2 style=\"font-size:1.35em;font-weight:600;margin:2.2em 0 0.7em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Important information</h2><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">Digital Capital, Digital Credit and Digital Equity describe the framework used in this article. STRC and SATA are preferred equity securities with different terms and issuer risks. A Bitcoin capital base does not by itself give investors a direct or secured claim on Bitcoin. The potential effects on asset values, funding costs, valuations and growth are forward-looking views, not assured outcomes. Prices, liquidity and dividends are not guaranteed, and investors can lose principal. Review each issuer’s filings and the applicable security’s prospectus.</span></p>"},{"uid":"blt0000000000000001","title":"How Strategy Engineers Digital Credit","author":"Michael J Saylor","date":"2026-09-29","url":"/media/articles/how-strategy-engineers-digital-credit","thumbnail":{"url":"https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltf8d808d9b8cebd37/blt26515a4d0232f2f9/howStrategyEngineersDigitalCredit.jpeg"},"content":"<p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Stripping volatility. Compressing duration. Extracting yield from Bitcoin.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>Bitcoin is Digital Capital. MSTR is Digital Equity. STRC is Digital Credit.</strong></p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Our corporate strategy is to create two complementary products from Bitcoin capital: MSTR, offering Amplified Bitcoin and ownership in a growing Digital Credit business; and STRC, designed to damp volatility, compress duration and deliver a USD yield.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Creating Digital Credit requires active management of an entire balance sheet: Bitcoin, dollars, debt, preferred stock and common equity. It requires decisions about capital, liquidity, seniority, dividend rates, payment frequency and the terms investors own.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Our ambition is to engineer the highest quality Digital Credit: attractive dollar income supported by financial resilience, disciplined capital allocation and a more stable investor experience.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The dividend is the visible output. The quality of the system behind it is the essential work.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>We manage the capital. We manage the claims. We manage the liquidity. We engineer the product.</strong></p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">One capital foundation. Two investment propositions.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Investors seeking Bitcoin price exposure can hold BTC or a spot Bitcoin fund. MSTR investors purchase equity in a company pursuing two sources of value: amplified exposure to Bitcoin and the growth of a Digital Credit business.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Through MSTR, we seek enhanced long-term performance by actively building Bitcoin capital, developing credit products and allocating capital productively. Equity investors participate in that opportunity while accepting amplified volatility and downside risk. Amplification works in both directions.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">STRC investors seek a different experience: dollar income, reduced price volatility and shorter-duration characteristics. We seek to serve that demand through the strength of our capital, the priority of the preferred claim, dollar liquidity and active management.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The two propositions are connected. The capital structure directs more of Bitcoin’s volatility and return potential toward common equity, helping support a more stable income proposition for credit investors. MSTR shareholders own the company that designs, issues and manages that credit.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The capital beneath a credit instrument helps absorb losses. The cash available to the company helps meet payments. The amount, cost and priority of every claim influence the resilience of the whole structure.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">We manage one balance sheet to create amplified exposure for equity investors and damped exposure for credit investors. Both propositions depend on the strength of the company and the quality of its execution.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">We build Bitcoin capital and dollar capacity.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Common equity gives us two distinct tools:</p><ul style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Issue MSTR to acquire BTC.</strong> This adds Bitcoin assets without creating another senior payment claim.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Issue MSTR to acquire USD.</strong> This can strengthen payment reserves, fund the retirement of outstanding claims or preserve capital for future opportunities.</li></ul><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Bitcoin provides long-term capital exposure. Dollars provide immediate capacity to pay, repurchase securities and act on opportunities. The appropriate balance depends on financing terms, market conditions and the company’s commitments.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Every common-equity issuance must be evaluated against dilution and long-term value per share. We seek to deploy the proceeds in ways that strengthen the company and improve its economics for shareholders.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">We manage STRC supply in both directions.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Issuance and repurchases allow us to adjust the amount of STRC outstanding as conditions change.</p><ul style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Above par, we can issue STRC.</strong> When the economics justify expansion, issuance brings capital into the company. We evaluate the proceeds against the preferred claims and future dividend requirements created.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Below par, we can repurchase STRC.</strong> Repurchases retire preferred shares and their associated future dividends at a discount to stated amount. They can improve the relationship between assets, outstanding claims and payment requirements.</li></ul><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Each decision depends on the price, available liquidity, funding costs and alternative uses of capital. Both tools remain subject to applicable restrictions, and repurchases are discretionary.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The discipline is to raise capital on attractive terms and retire claims when doing so is the better use of capital. A buyback policy supports that discipline; it does not establish a guaranteed price floor.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">We manage every layer of the capital structure.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">STRC’s position depends on the claims above and below it. We manage those layers together.</p><ul style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Bonds rank ahead of preferred equity.</strong> Refinancing, repurchasing or redeeming bonds can change senior claims, financing costs and the timing of cash requirements. We consider stated maturities and dates when holders may require repayment.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>STRF is senior to STRC.</strong> We can issue STRF, pause issuance, or pursue repurchases or redemptions when permitted. Additional senior financing brings in assets while adding claims ahead of STRC.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>STRK, STRE and STRD are junior to STRC.</strong> We can issue these instruments, pause issuance, or pursue their retirement when permitted. Junior financing can add assets without adding a preferred claim ahead of STRC, while introducing its own financing costs and terms.</li></ul><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Retiring a senior claim may strengthen STRC’s position, but it consumes liquidity. Issuing a junior instrument may add capital beneath STRC’s priority, but its dividends, conversion features and other terms still matter.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">We evaluate each transaction by its effect on the whole company. Redemption rights remain governed by each security’s terms; pausing issuance does not change the rights of existing holders.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">We give payment reserves and allocation cash different jobs.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Dollar liquidity serves two distinct purposes:</p><ul style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>USD Reserve supports payment continuity.</strong> It is designated for preferred dividends and interest on outstanding debt.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>USD Cash supports capital allocation.</strong> It is available for Bitcoin treasury purposes, including debt buybacks, preferred buybacks, common-equity buybacks and Bitcoin purchases. It excludes the payment reserve and cash for ordinary operating needs.</li></ul><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This distinction keeps us from counting the same dollar as both payment coverage and freely deployable investment capital.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">We adjust the reserve in relation to the payments it supports. A larger reserve can extend coverage. Retiring dividend-bearing shares can reduce the payment burden. Raising a dividend rate increases that burden.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">We also evaluate how to replenish cash. Depending on economics and existing authorizations, sources can include financing and selective Bitcoin monetization. Payment capacity must exist in dollars when dollars are needed.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>Strong capital supports credit. Available cash supports payments. We manage both.</strong></p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">We manage the dividend rate within the whole system.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">STRC’s adjustable dividend rate is an important part of its design. We consider the rate alongside market price, competing yields, credit spreads, Bitcoin conditions, reserve coverage and the broader capital structure.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">A higher rate may attract more demand, but it also increases payment requirements. Other responses may include repurchasing shares, building reserves, reducing senior claims or changing issuance activity.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The objective is an attractive income proposition supported by a resilient financial structure. Rate decisions must serve that objective while seeking to support trading near the stated amount.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">We keep improving the security itself.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Payment frequency, dividend-rate mechanics and other terms shape the investor’s experience. They also affect how financial institutions can use the instrument in their own products.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Our proposal for daily dividends on U.S.-listed preferred securities illustrates this approach. If approved and adopted, dividends would accrue on every calendar day, including weekends and holidays, and be payable on the next business day when declared.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The objective is to shorten the interval between earning income and receiving cash, improve reinvestment timing and increase the usefulness of the securities for investors and product providers.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">More frequent payments change the timing of income. They do not create daily redemption rights or guarantee stable principal.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">We can propose amendments, refine policies and improve the operating design as the market develops, subject to required approvals. Product development continues after issuance.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">We seek shorter duration and a longer payment runway.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">For the investor, the goal is to reduce relevant price sensitivity and improve the timing of cash flows. An adjustable dividend rate can reduce certain interest-rate sensitivities relative to a comparable fixed-rate instrument. More frequent payments bring income forward.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">For the company, a longer payment runway provides more capacity to meet commitments without depending on an immediate financing transaction or asset sale.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>Shorter duration for the investor. Longer payment coverage for the issuer.</strong></p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">These objectives address different risks. STRC remains perpetual and sensitive to the issuer’s credit and market conditions. A dividend-rate adjustment does not create a maturity date or a promise to return principal.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">The levers work together.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The value of the management toolkit comes from coordinating its parts.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Consider a hypothetical period when STRC trades below par and MSTR issuance offers attractive economics. Raising common equity and using part of the proceeds to repurchase STRC could retire preferred claims and reduce future dividends. Reserving another portion in dollars could improve payment coverage.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">A different environment might favor STRC issuance above par, additional Bitcoin purchases and reserve growth. Another might favor bond refinancing, a pause in senior preferred issuance or retaining cash for a future opportunity.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">We can adjust Digital Credit policies and the overall mix of Bitcoin, dollars, debt, preferred stock and common equity through appropriate governance. Those choices determine how individual transactions fit together.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Every action must be assessed against assets, claims, payment requirements, dilution and future flexibility. Sometimes preserving the ability to act later is the most valuable decision.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">MSTR shareholders own the Digital Credit business.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The equity proposition combines Amplified Bitcoin with ownership in a company building a financial business around Digital Credit.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Shareholders participate in the potential appreciation of our Bitcoin capital and in the value we can create through product innovation, broader investor adoption, financing capacity and disciplined capital allocation. Each successful improvement can make our credit more useful and expand the opportunity for the business.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Our ambition is to build a major source of reserve capital and Digital Credit for the crypto economy. MSTR gives investors ownership in that institution.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">As demand for Digital Credit grows, attractive financing can support Bitcoin accumulation, strengthen financial flexibility and expand our capacity to develop additional products. The opportunity for common shareholders is to participate in the growth of both the capital base and the business built around it.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">That growth must create value per common share. Its benefits must exceed the full economic cost of financing, including dilution, payment requirements and the cost of maintaining liquidity.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">In turn, a stronger common-equity capital base can improve the resilience of the preferred structure.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>Stronger capital supports better Digital Credit. Better Digital Credit can expand the business. Disciplined growth can create greater value for MSTR shareholders.</strong></p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Credit quality and equity value are connected objectives. Our job is to make them reinforce each other.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Digital Credit is a discipline we practice.</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Our objective has three parts:</p><ul style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Strip volatility.</strong> Seek to reduce how much Bitcoin’s price movements affect the credit investor through capital, liquidity, seniority and active management.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Compress duration.</strong> Improve cash-flow timing and reduce relevant price sensitivity while managing the continuing risks of perpetual credit.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Extract yield.</strong> Transform Bitcoin capital into an income-producing corporate security through financing, reserves and disciplined capital allocation.</li></ul><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Bitcoin itself pays no coupon. Strategy pays dividends under the terms of its securities. The income-producing instrument is the result of the corporate structure and the management system supporting it.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Better Digital Credit can provide a foundation for funds, tokenized securities and products designed to combine income with dollar stability. Each additional structure must establish its own liquidity, protections and investor economics.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Every capital raise, repurchase, reserve decision, dividend adjustment and product improvement serves the same objective: stronger Digital Credit and greater long-term value for our shareholders.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>Bitcoin is Digital Capital.</strong></p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>Strategy engineers Digital Credit.</strong></p><h2 style=\"font-size:1.35em;font-weight:600;margin:2.2em 0 0.7em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Important information</h2><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">“Highest quality” describes our design ambition, not an independent credit rating or a guarantee. STRC is perpetual preferred equity, not a bank deposit or a direct claim on pledged Bitcoin. Investors can lose principal; market price, liquidity and cash dividends are not guaranteed. Repurchases and policies are discretionary, and proposed amendments require applicable approvals. Statements about objectives and expected benefits are forward-looking and subject to risks described in Strategy’s SEC filings. Investors should review the applicable prospectuses and, for proposed dividend amendments, the proxy materials.</span></p>"},{"uid":"blta9da715685f14014","title":"Prescriptions for Prosperity in the Digital Economy","author":"Michael J Saylor","date":"2026-09-26","url":"/media/articles/prescriptions-for-prosperity-in-the-digital-economy","thumbnail":{"url":"https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltf8d808d9b8cebd37/blt963b4e10eb0ad00c/prescriptionsForProsperity.jpeg"},"content":"<p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">The age of Digital Assets and Digital Intelligence needs a bill of digital rights, not a bill of restrictions.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Artificial intelligence will make it possible for individuals and companies to produce far more than they can today. That makes the freedom to create, finance, own, and exchange things more important. A more productive economy needs better money and better capital markets to realize its potential.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">At the Bitcoin Policy Institute's Freedom Tech DC summit, I discussed these ideas with Conner Brown. My central policy recommendation is straightforward: individuals and companies need the right to create, issue, custody, transfer, and use digital assets to build wealth and prosperity.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The age of Digital Assets and Digital Intelligence needs a bill of digital rights, not a bill of restrictions.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Begin With the Rights of Individuals and Companies</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Freedom starts with the ability to act. A useful framework for digital assets should establish five fundamental rights.</p><ul style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Create:</strong> Develop new digital assets, financial instruments, and applications.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Issue:</strong> Bring those assets to market and use them to finance businesses and productive activity.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Custody:</strong> Hold assets directly or choose a custodian that offers the best service.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Transfer:</strong> Move assets between people, companies, wallets, and service providers.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Use:</strong> Spend, invest, earn income, and borrow against assets.</li></ul><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">These rights should belong to individuals and corporations alike. They need a foundation of financial privacy and practical access to markets. An asset's value depends on what its owner can do with it. Restrict its usefulness, and you restrict its economic potential.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Digital tokens, digital currency, digital capital, and digital securities perform different economic functions. Policy should recognize those differences while preserving a common foundation of ownership and freedom.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Clear disclosure, enforceable ownership, and accountability for fraud support functioning markets. Rules should make it easier for honest participants to transact with confidence. They should also leave room for products and business models that do not yet exist.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Make It Possible to Finance 10 Million New Companies</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Digital intelligence will automate jobs, transform industries, and make established products obsolete. Prosperity will depend on our ability to create new businesses and new opportunities at an even greater pace.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">A person who can build a product with AI should also be able to finance the company that brings it to market. The cost, complexity, and delay of raising capital should fall as the technology for creating businesses improves.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Digital tokens offer a way to make capital formation faster and less expensive. Policymakers should establish clear, practical issuance rules, proportionate disclosure requirements, and straightforward ways for entrepreneurs to reach prospective investors. Financing a small business should be accessible to people who cannot afford an army of lawyers.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Our ambition should be to enable 10 million new companies to raise capital. That is how the productivity of digital intelligence can become new employment, new products, and broadly shared prosperity.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Protecting existing business models while making it difficult to finance their successors leaves the economy poorly prepared for technological change.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Let the Digital Dollar Compete</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Digital currency can put dollars into the hands of people around the world and allow them to move at the speed of light.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">If we want the dollar to succeed, we should want the best companies competing to make it useful. Banks, financial technology companies, and technology platforms should have a clear path to offer digital dollars. Imagine the reach of dollar products built into the devices and applications billions of people already use.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Issuers should also be allowed to compete on yield. Customers should be able to choose among products with different returns, services, and clearly disclosed risks. A policy that suppresses yield to protect institutions paying little or no interest puts the interests of those institutions ahead of their customers.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">My recommendation is to permit that competition. Where the law prevents it, the law should change.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The United States has an opportunity to expand the dollar's usefulness and reach by allowing American companies to build better products around it.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Bring Bitcoin Into Banking and Insurance</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Bitcoin is Digital Capital. Its usefulness increases when individuals and businesses can hold it securely, finance it efficiently, and integrate it into the rest of the economy.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Banks should be able to custody Bitcoin and extend credit against it under clear, commercially workable rules. Insurance companies should have a practical path to incorporate digital capital into their balance sheets and product design. Competition should encourage them to improve benefits and lower costs for customers.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This requires reviewing accounting, capital, and supervisory rules that make these activities unnecessarily difficult. The Basel framework's 1,250 percent risk weight for Group 2b cryptoasset exposures illustrates the severity of some existing capital treatment. <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://www.bis.org/committees/bcbs/basel-framework/standard/sco/60/inforce/2026-01-01/published/2024-11-27\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">BIS</a>)</span> I believe policymakers should revisit that treatment and assess digital assets according to their actual risks and the activity involved.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Holding an asset for a customer, lending against collateral, and taking a position on a bank's own balance sheet are different activities. Regulation should distinguish them.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">When more institutions compete to serve Bitcoin owners, those owners gain more ways to use their capital without selling it. Businesses gain access to financing, financial institutions gain customers, and digital capital becomes more productive within the economy.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">I expect bank adoption to be a major driver of the industry's growth. As banks compete to provide custody and credit, more capital can enter a market whose central asset, Bitcoin, has a limited supply.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Make Tokenization Expand the Rights of the Owner</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Tokenized securities can make equity and credit available around the clock and across markets. Their greatest potential lies in what they allow owners to do.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">An investor should be able to hold a tokenized security directly, transfer it to a preferred service provider, and use it in a competitive market for custody and credit. A company should have those rights as well.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Consider an investor with $1 million of stock. One provider might offer better financing terms; another might offer an income opportunity; a third might provide better service. The investor should be able to compare those choices and move the asset accordingly.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Self-custody matters even to people who ultimately choose a custodian. The ability to leave gives the customer bargaining power. If assets can move, providers must compete to retain them. That competition can improve service, reduce borrowing costs, and give owners more of the economic value their assets generate.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Simply putting a security on a blockchain while confining it to the same closed group of intermediaries leaves much of this opportunity unrealized. The policy objective should be to expand the owner's choices.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Protect Financial Privacy</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Financial privacy is part of economic freedom. Individuals should be able to live their lives, and companies should be able to conduct routine business, without unnecessary disclosure of their financial affairs. Protecting that privacy also protects personal security, commercial strategy, and the freedom to choose whom to do business with.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">My policy preference is clear: ordinary, lawful transactions below a meaningful threshold, such as $10,000, should not trigger routine government reporting solely because money or digital assets have moved. Reporting should serve a defined public purpose and impose a burden proportionate to the risk. Privacy in ordinary commerce can coexist with targeted reporting and investigation of suspicious activity.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The familiar federal currency-transaction reporting rule applies to cash transactions over $10,000, including transactions aggregated under the rules. <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://www.fincen.gov/sites/default/files/shared/CTRPamphlet.pdf\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">FinCEN</a>)</span> That threshold dates to 1972. In a 2024 report, the Government Accountability Office estimated that an inflation-adjusted threshold would have been approximately $72,880 in 2023. <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-25-106500\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">GAO</a>)</span> Leaving a threshold unchanged for decades subjects increasingly ordinary economic activity to a system designed for much larger transactions.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Policymakers should raise outdated reporting thresholds and index them to inflation. A digital economy also needs clear protections for routine transfers between people, businesses, and their own accounts or wallets. The ability to move an asset efficiently and privately is part of what makes it useful.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Make Compliance Portable</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">In over-the-counter markets, the same investor can be asked to complete a separate anti-money-laundering and know-your-customer process with each financial counterparty. Documents are collected again, identities are checked again, and approvals can take days. Each additional relationship carries a cost before any productive activity begins.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">We should aspire to billions of investors transacting with millions of providers in seconds at negligible cost. A system that requires every relationship to begin with another manual review can leave us with the opposite: thousands of investors, dozens of providers, days of delay, and great expense. These are competing visions for the scale and accessibility of finance.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Policymakers should make it practical to verify identity once and reuse trusted credentials across providers, with the customer's permission and appropriate updates. Existing bank rules already permit limited reliance on another financial institution's identity-verification procedures. <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-X/part-1020/subpart-B/section-1020.220\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">eCFR</a>)</span> We should expand practical reliance, establish clear responsibility and liability, and support interoperable credentials that disclose only the information needed for a transaction.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Providers would remain responsible for assessing risk and monitoring suspicious activity. But routine verification should be reusable, and additional scrutiny should follow actual risk. Collecting the same sensitive documents repeatedly adds cost and creates more copies of information that must be protected.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Lower onboarding costs would make it easier for investors to compare providers, for new firms to win customers, and for businesses to obtain capital. Privacy and competition reinforce each other when customers can prove what is necessary without surrendering more information than the service requires.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Make Digital Money Practical to Use</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The right to use an asset must work in ordinary life. Buying dinner or paying for a routine service should not turn a customer into a tax accountant. Under current U.S. tax rules, spending a digital asset can require calculating and reporting a gain or loss. <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://www.irs.gov/filing/digital-assets\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">IRS</a>)</span> That administrative burden discourages everyday use.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Policymakers should establish a meaningful de minimis exemption for ordinary digital asset payments. A $20 or $200 cap on the value of a purchase is inadequate for modern commerce. A family dinner can exceed $200. Calling a token allowance financial freedom understates what citizens need to participate in a digital economy.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The design matters. A threshold based on taxable gain is different from a limit on the value of a purchase. Relief should be large enough to cover ordinary spending, indexed to inflation, and simple enough to eliminate needless transaction-by-transaction calculations and recordkeeping for qualifying payments.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Tax exemptions and government reporting thresholds solve different problems. Both should respect citizens' time and the economics of everyday life. An asset that moves instantly but creates hours of paperwork has not delivered on the promise of digital money.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Build a Financial System That AI Agents Can Use</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">We are moving toward an economy in which software performs more of the work people once did through phone calls, websites, and face-to-face meetings. AI agents will increasingly research, negotiate, purchase, and coordinate with other agents.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">That economy needs financial infrastructure that operates continuously. Money and capital must be available at the speed of software, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The traditional financial system is organized around human identities, human interfaces, and human working hours. As individuals and companies delegate more activity to AI, they will need practical ways for their agents to transact on their behalf. That means digital wallets, programmable payments, transferable assets, and financial services that software can access directly.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Bitcoin and other digital assets fit naturally into that environment. An agent operating across the internet needs capital it can recognize and use digitally. It cannot move a bar of gold at the speed of light or wait months for a property transaction every time it needs to allocate resources.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Digital intelligence will increase the amount of productive activity that can take place. Digital assets can help finance and coordinate that activity. Their intersection is where I expect much of the next wave of innovation to emerge.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Make Technological Capability a National Priority</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">AI will create risks as well as opportunities. Some people will use powerful technology for harmful purposes. The response should be to ensure that responsible individuals, companies, and public institutions have the capability to defend themselves.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">If a hostile actor uses an AI agent, an effective defense may require a better agent. A country that limits its own technological development cannot assume its adversaries will accept the same limits.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">We understand this with air power, space power, and cyber power. National security depends on the ability to develop and deploy advanced technology.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">America should put the best tools into the hands of its people, businesses, schools, and public institutions. We should enable students to learn with AI and entrepreneurs to build with it. The ability to solve a problem more effectively is a reason to develop a technology's potential.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Technological leadership requires broad participation. Every capable person we enable becomes another source of invention, productivity, and resilience.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Let Regulators Lead Where They Can Act</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Over the next two years, I believe the most promising path to greater digital asset freedom runs through the SEC, the CFTC, Treasury, and the White House.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The SEC should make capital formation and tokenized securities more useful and accessible. The CFTC should enable competitive digital commodity and derivatives markets. Treasury and the banking regulators should establish workable paths for custody, credit, payments, and the integration of digital capital into financial institutions. The White House should coordinate a national direction that favors innovation and economic leadership.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Each institution should use its lawful authority to remove unnecessary barriers and establish clear paths for new products. Where legislation is required, Congress should extend the rights of individuals and companies.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">My objection to the approach taken in CLARITY is that it placed too much emphasis on restrictions. The test for any proposal should be what people will be able to create, own, transfer, and use after it takes effect.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">A long, detailed law can still be a poor foundation for prosperity if it protects existing intermediaries by limiting the usefulness of new assets. Certainty has little value when it makes productive innovation impossible.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Build the Products That Make Freedom Durable</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">One argument for comprehensive legislation is that it could protect the industry from a hostile future administration. That is a reasonable goal. But a law that eliminates most of the industry's potential at the outset is an expensive form of protection.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">There is another source of durability: useful products that people depend on.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Washington finds it difficult to defend a product that does not yet exist for customers who have not yet appeared. Once millions of people use that product to save money, finance a business, or improve their lives, its value becomes tangible. Those customers have something concrete to defend.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The industry should build excellent products, bring them to market, and earn that support. Policymakers should give it room to do so. We can refine rules as markets develop and actual problems become clear.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">I believe digital assets can grow into a $100 trillion industry. Reaching that potential will require millions of people and companies experimenting with better ways to create and organize capital.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Give them the right to create, issue, custody, transfer, and use digital assets. Let them compete to make those assets more useful. <strong>That is how we create wealth and prosperity in the age of intelligence.</strong></p><h2 style=\"font-size:1.35em;font-weight:600;margin:2.2em 0 0.7em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Sources and Further Reading</h2><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This essay draws on the Basel Framework's treatment of Group 2b cryptoasset exposures, FinCEN's currency-transaction-reporting guidance, the Government Accountability Office's 2024 report on currency transaction reports, the federal rules on reliance for customer identification, and IRS guidance on digital assets. <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://www.bis.org/committees/bcbs/basel-framework/standard/sco/60/inforce/2026-01-01/published/2024-11-27\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">BIS</a>, <a href=\"https://www.fincen.gov/sites/default/files/shared/CTRPamphlet.pdf\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">FinCEN</a>, <a href=\"https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-25-106500\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">GAO</a>, <a href=\"https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-X/part-1020/subpart-B/section-1020.220\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">eCFR</a>, <a href=\"https://www.irs.gov/filing/digital-assets\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">IRS</a>)</span></p>\n"},{"uid":"blte28b176daa1c44ce","title":"Digital Assets After CLARITY: The Best Protection Is Adoption","author":"Michael J Saylor","date":"2026-09-19","url":"/media/articles/digital-assets-after-clarity-the-best-protection-is-adoption","thumbnail":{"url":"https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltf8d808d9b8cebd37/blt59d8744c9ecadfd1/DigitalAssetsClarityAct.jpeg"},"content":"<p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Lower costs, easier access, and greater control over money create the constituency that protects innovation.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The Digital Assets industry is better off moving forward with supportive rules from the SEC, CFTC, Treasury, and banking regulators than accepting the restrictions in the final CLARITY compromise. We have an administration willing to modernize financial markets. We should use the next two years to put better financial products into people's hands.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Our safest path forward is to create products that delight customers and deploy them broadly. Lower costs, easier access, useful services, and greater control over money give people a direct interest in preserving innovation. The strongest constituency we can build is a public that benefits from what we create.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Legal certainty matters. So does the freedom to compete. A law can make a restriction durable just as easily as it can make a right durable. Before celebrating permanence, we should examine what we are making permanent.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">What CLARITY Would Have Restricted</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The September CLARITY compromise would have restricted covered providers from paying customers simply for holding payment stablecoins, while allowing qualifying activity rewards. It also would have directed Treasury to restrict certain rewards upon specified findings of substantial, detrimental deposit transfers from community banks. <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://www.lummis.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/EHF26724.pdf\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">Lummis Senate</a>)</span></p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Protecting a bank from a liquidity crisis and protecting it from a better competitor are different objectives. Financial stability requires sound oversight. Competition requires that customers be free to choose a better service. When technology reduces the cost of delivering financial services, consumers should share in the savings.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The separate GENIUS Act already contains restrictions on issuer-paid stablecoin interest and yield, subject to its effective-date provisions. <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/12/5903\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">Cornell Law</a>)</span> CLARITY's setback leaves that law intact. The issue is whether to layer additional restrictions onto providers and rewards.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Even CLARITY's innovation sandbox would have limited participating firms to 25 employees and each commission to 20 project approvals annually. <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://www.lummis.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/EHF26724.pdf#page=247\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">Lummis Senate</a>)</span> These were limits on that program, but they illustrate how legislation can fix the dimensions of an experiment before the market has revealed its potential.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The objective should be a free market in financial innovation: clear rules, open entry, vigorous competition, and freedom for customers to choose. Protect ownership rights, require honest disclosures, and punish fraud. Within those rules, let entrepreneurs test better technologies and business models, and let successful products grow.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">The Administration Is Already Opening That Path</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">On September 17, the SEC used existing authority to provide conditional relief for onchain trading of certain tokenized stocks. Chairman Paul Atkins described a process of allowing markets to develop, learning from their operation, and following temporary relief with durable rulemaking. Investor protections and the securities laws' prohibitions on fraud remain in place. <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/speeches-statements/atkins-innovation-exemption-bridge-toward-durable-rulemaking-091726\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">SEC</a>)</span></p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">CFTC Chairman Michael Selig supported CLARITY, but also committed to using existing authority if the bill stalled. He directed staff to explore rules for leveraged or margined crypto trading through regulated markets and to work with developers on lawful onchain finance. <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://www.cftc.gov/PressRoom/SpeechesTestimony/opaselig10\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">CFTC</a>)</span></p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has connected stablecoin implementation with innovation, American growth, and the dollar's global role. Workable rules can help translate those objectives into payments, commerce, and financial services people use. <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0605\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">Treasury</a>)</span></p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">CLARITY itself preserved existing SEC exemptive authority. <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://www.lummis.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/EHF26724.pdf#page=116\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">Lummis Senate</a>)</span> That is precisely the point: substantial opportunities already exist under current law. We can pursue them without accepting the bill's additional restrictions as the price of progress.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">The Digital Assets Stack</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">As appropriate rules and compliant market infrastructure develop, the benefits can extend across the Digital Assets economy.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>Digital Capital—Bitcoin (BTC).</strong> The OCC has eased supervisory barriers to bank crypto custody. <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/news-releases/2025/nr-occ-2025-16.html\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">OCC</a>)</span> Building on that progress with workable custody rules and prudently underwritten lending can make Bitcoin easier to own, finance, and use as collateral. More institutions competing to serve Bitcoin holders can expand access and deepen liquidity.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>Digital Credit—Stretch (STRC).</strong> Our flagship Digital Credit instrument, STRC, is preferred stock that connects Strategy's Bitcoin treasury business with investors seeking income. <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://www.strategy.com/strc/brief\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">Strategy</a>)</span> Supportive rules can open opportunities for broader distribution, tokenized ownership, and more convenient trading while preserving shareholders' legal rights. Compliant lending arrangements could make STRC more useful as collateral, with clear terms and risk disclosures.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>Digital Equity—Strategy (MSTR).</strong> Additional compliant trading venues, easier transfer, and longer trading hours could widen participation in Strategy's common stock and improve liquidity. More efficient access to equity capital can help Bitcoin treasury companies finance growth and develop new financial products. Modernizing market infrastructure can benefit both issuers and shareholders.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>Digital Exchanges—Coinbase (COIN).</strong> Platforms such as Coinbase can compete to combine crypto, securities, custody, payments, and financing in a more useful customer experience. <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://www.coinbase.com/about\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">Coinbase</a>)</span> Supportive rules can help appropriately regulated businesses introduce and integrate new products. Broader participation creates business opportunities for exchanges and greater competition on price and service for customers.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>Digital Currency—Circle (USDC).</strong> USDC, the regulated dollar stablecoin issued through affiliates of U.S.-based Circle, connects digital finance to everyday payments and global commerce. <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://www.circle.com/usdc\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">Circle</a>)</span> Supportive rules can help Circle and its partners expand digital dollar use through faster settlement, programmable payments, and integration with financial institutions. American businesses can gain new markets while the dollar becomes more useful worldwide.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>Digital Innovation.</strong> These categories reinforce one another. Capital supports credit. Equity finances businesses. Exchanges connect investors and issuers. Digital currency moves value between them. Developers can combine these capabilities into products more useful than the individual components. Open competition lets more people build, more ideas be tested, and more value reach customers.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Banks should participate in this future. They can compete to provide custody, payments, distribution, and credit against digital assets. Established institutions and new entrants should earn customers by delivering better products and service. That is how financial innovation improves the financial system.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Why Speed Matters</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Speed matters because innovation compounds. An earlier launch produces earlier feedback. Better products attract customers, distribution, and investment, which support the next round of improvement. A year spent waiting is a year of benefits customers never receive and experience American businesses never acquire.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The gains extend beyond finance. Lower payment and financing costs can free resources for businesses to invest, hire, and expand. Faster settlement puts capital back to work sooner. Broader access connects savers and entrepreneurs. Giving American firms room to develop and export these capabilities can strengthen the U.S. economy while creating value around the world.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">The Best Protection Is a Public That Benefits</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The strongest argument for CLARITY is familiar: \"We need a law to protect us from a future hostile administration.\"</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Durable law can protect rights, and some changes still require Congress. But no statute removes politics from regulation. A future administration would still make important implementation and enforcement decisions. The industry also needs a public constituency that makes hostility costly.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Imagine 50 million American voters using digital financial products that improve their lives: cheaper payments, convenient access to Bitcoin, useful securities, transparent income products, and credit on competitive terms.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Those voters would have something concrete to defend. Taking away an unfamiliar technology is politically different from taking away a service millions of people rely on. A future administration would have to explain why those customers should lose benefits they already enjoy.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The goal should be 50 million satisfied users with a direct interest in preserving financial choice. Adoption raises the political cost of reversal. Sound rulemaking strengthens the legal foundation. We should build both.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Adoption also improves the next legislative debate. Products that do not yet exist have no customers to speak for them. Once they are widely used, households, businesses, advisers, developers, and banks can explain what they want preserved. A record of public benefit gives the industry a stronger position than promises about what it might someday deliver.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Customer delight must be earned. Products should be useful, understandable, and dependable in good markets and difficult ones. Transparent terms, honest risk disclosures, convenient access, and the freedom to change providers build trust. Broad deployment turns that trust into lasting support.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">We should use 2027 and 2028 to establish useful products at scale, convert temporary relief into durable rules, and pursue focused legislation where additional authority or protections are needed. The measure of success is the value delivered to customers and the economy.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Let the Digital Assets industry innovate rapidly in a free market and create the greatest possible value for the U.S. and global economy. Create products that delight customers. Deploy them broadly. Give millions of people a reason to defend the freedom that made them possible.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>The best protection for digital innovation is a public that benefits from it.</strong></p>\n"},{"uid":"blt91ea671c6d9940f3","title":"The Bitcoin Reformation","author":"Michael J. Saylor","date":"2026-08-24","url":"/media/articles/the-bitcoin-reformation","thumbnail":{"url":"https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltf8d808d9b8cebd37/blt839ae041aa2cc2bf/The-Bitcoin-Reformation.png"},"content":"<p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Bitcoin began as an act of technological dissent. It will reach its full potential as an architecture of economic inclusion.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Bitcoin is approaching a decisive transition. The network that began as an experiment among cryptographers has become a global capital system used by individuals, funds, public companies, banks, custodians, exchanges, and governments.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Yet a portion of the culture still evaluates this expanding economy through a narrow set of founding-era beliefs: Satoshi must be treated as an oracle; the white paper must answer every question; Bitcoin must become everyday currency; self-custody is the only authentic form of ownership; governments and banks must disappear; and every security, credit instrument, or custodial claim built around bitcoin is merely \"paper Bitcoin.\"</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Those beliefs once served a purpose. Radical skepticism protected a fragile network before it had institutions, laws, professional custody, deep liquidity, or political legitimacy. But survival heuristics can harden into doctrine. What helps a movement survive infancy can prevent it from reaching maturity.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The choice is not between Bitcoin and institutions.
