Civilizational Memory</h2><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Will and Ariel Durant</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The historical backbone of this curriculum is Will and Ariel Durant’s The Story of Civilization, together with their concise synthesis, The Lessons of History.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The eleven-volume series begins with the civilizations of Asia and the ancient Near East, then proceeds through Greece, Rome, medieval civilization, the Renaissance, the Reformation, the Enlightenment, the French Revolution, and Napoleon.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The Durants show civilization as a dynamic system. Religion, family, commerce, banking, war, philosophy, technology, law, art, institutions, and exceptional individuals interact across centuries.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Ideas become institutions. Institutions accumulate power. Prosperity generates complexity. Success creates capability, but also complacency.</p><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">1. The Lessons of History</h4><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Estimated reading time: 3–5 hours</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This is the overture and the coda.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The Durants compress a lifetime of historical study into a short examination of geography, biology, morality, religion, economics, government, war, and social change.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Read it once before beginning the larger series, as a map of the territory. Read it again after completing the curriculum, when each observation will carry the weight of examples.</p><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">2. Our Oriental Heritage</h4><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Estimated reading time: 31–38 hours</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This volume establishes the Eastern and Near Eastern foundations of civilization, including Egypt, Mesopotamia, Persia, India, China, and Japan.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">It corrects an excessively Western conception of history. Writing, law, mathematics, bureaucracy, religion, commerce, philosophy, and imperial administration developed across many civilizations over thousands of years.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The first lesson of civilizational history is humility: no culture invented civilization by itself.</p><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">3. The Life of Greece</h4><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Estimated reading time: 22–27 hours</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This volume examines the Greek polis, philosophy, science, democracy, tragedy, sculpture, architecture, political rivalry, and war.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The Greek achievement was not merely a collection of great ideas. It was the creation of environments in which explanation, argument, criticism, and civic participation could flourish.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">It also demonstrates how faction, rhetoric, envy, and strategic overreach can destroy a society rich in intelligence and culture.</p><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">4. Caesar and Christ</h4><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Estimated reading time: 22–27 hours</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This volume traces the Roman Republic, Roman law, imperial administration, social order, military power, and the rise of Christianity within the empire.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Rome demonstrates that durable civilization requires more than conquest. It requires logistics, infrastructure, law, administration, legitimacy, and a shared conception of order.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Christianity’s emergence within the Roman system also shows how an initially marginal idea can eventually reorganize the moral structure of an empire.</p><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">5. The Age of Faith</h4><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Estimated reading time: 35–43 hours</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This volume examines Christianity, Islam, Byzantium, feudalism, monasticism, universities, scholastic philosophy, and the institutions that preserved order through political fragmentation.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The period commonly described as the Dark Ages was also an age of institutional reconstruction. Religious orders preserved knowledge. Commercial networks reemerged. Universities formed. Law evolved. Competing authorities constrained one another.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Read it to understand how civilization survives when centralized political order weakens or collapses.</p><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">6. The Renaissance</h4><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Estimated reading time: 23–28 hours</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This volume shows how cities, commerce, banking, patronage, humanism, and recovered antiquity released extraordinary creative energy.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The Renaissance was not merely an artistic movement. It was an economic and institutional phenomenon.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Capital, urban autonomy, competition, and patronage created environments in which talent could compound.</p><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">7. The Reformation</h4><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Estimated reading time: 30–37 hours</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This volume explores conscience, printing, religious authority, political centralization, and the destruction of a unified Western Christendom.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The printing press radically reduced the cost of distributing ideas. Dissent became scalable. Competing interpretations of truth escaped centralized control.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The Reformation demonstrates both the liberating and destabilizing effects of information technology.</p><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">8. The Age of Reason Begins</h4><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Estimated reading time: 22–26 hours</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This volume follows the transition from confessional conflict toward scientific inquiry, political realism, and the centralized state.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Civilization began to separate questions settled by authority from questions requiring observation, experimentation, and reason.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">At the same time, the state acquired greater capacity to tax, administer, regulate, mobilize, and wage war.</p><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">9. The Age of Louis XIV</h4><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Estimated reading time: 24–29 hours</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This volume studies absolutism, court culture, public finance, administration, warfare, and the European balance of power.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Louis XIV’s France demonstrates the power and danger of centralization.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The state became culturally and militarily formidable, but grandeur brought fiscal exhaustion and institutional brittleness.</p><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">10. The Age of Voltaire</h4><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Estimated reading time: 24–29 hours</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This volume examines the Enlightenment critique of inherited authority, superstition, intolerance, and institutional privilege.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Authority increasingly had to justify itself through reason rather than tradition alone.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Read it to understand the intellectual foundations of liberalism, religious tolerance, scientific confidence, and the modern challenge to arbitrary power.</p><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">11. Rousseau and Revolution</h4><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Estimated reading time: 32–39 hours</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This volume explores the collision among reason, sentiment, equality, legitimacy, and revolutionary pressure.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Rousseau redirected political thought toward authenticity, popular sovereignty, equality, and collective will.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Those ideas inspired liberation, but also supplied new justifications for coercion in the name of the people.</p><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">12. The Age of Napoleon</h4><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Estimated reading time: 26–31 hours</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This volume shows how revolutionary energy became empire, codified law, administrative modernization, nationalism, and continental war.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Napoleon institutionalized many achievements of the Revolution while subordinating them to military ambition and personal power.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Read it as a study of leadership, state capacity, meritocracy, propaganda, strategic genius, and the tendency of concentrated power to outrun its limits.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The Durants should be read as architects of a grand synthesis, not as the final authority on every historical detail. Some scholarship and framing are dated. Their enduring value is scale: they teach the reader to see civilization as the interaction of religion, family, commerce, war, technology, art, institutions, and individuals over centuries.</p><h2 style=\"font-size:1.35em;font-weight:600;margin:2.2em 0 0.7em 0;line-height:1.3;\">II. Geography, Ecology, and Uneven Development</h2><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Jared Diamond</h3><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">13. Guns, Germs, and Steel</h4><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Estimated reading time: 18–24 hours</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Diamond asks a fundamental question: Why did wealth, military power, technology, and political organization develop unevenly across human societies?</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">His model emphasizes geography, climate, food production, domesticable plants and animals, disease exposure, population density, continental orientation, and the diffusion of technology.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This perspective matters because leaders routinely overestimate intention and underestimate inherited conditions.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">A society does not choose its geography, natural resources, navigable rivers, disease environment, or initial inventory of domesticable species. These factors shape population, trade, military capacity, institutional development, and the rate at which knowledge can spread.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The book also supplies an important corrective to racial explanations of conquest. Differences in civilizational outcomes do not require differences in human intelligence or worth.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">But Guns, Germs, and Steel should be treated as a model, not a complete causal theory.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Geography influences history. It does not write history by itself. Human agency, institutions, culture, leadership, ideology, trade, property rights, and deliberate acts of conquest remain consequential.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Some scholars have criticized Diamond for environmental determinism and for reducing the role of human decisions and Indigenous agency. That criticism should be included in the reading, not hidden from it. A persuasive grand theory is most educational when the reader also learns where it overreaches.</p><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">(<a href=\"https://books.apple.com/us/book/guns-germs-and-steel/id1207409071?utm_source=chatgpt.com\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">Apple</a>)</p><h2 style=\"font-size:1.35em;font-weight:600;margin:2.2em 0 0.7em 0;line-height:1.3;\">III. War, Strategy, and Republican Power</h2><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">War is one of civilization’s oldest and most destructive institutions.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">It has created states, dissolved empires, accelerated technology, rearranged borders, destroyed capital, and transferred power across cultures.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">A leader who does not understand war may start one believing it will be brief, rational, and controllable. The Prize</h4><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Estimated reading time: 27–36 hours</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Yergin follows the history of oil and its relationship to industrialization, transportation, warfare, national power, corporate organization, and the world economy.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Modern civilization rests on energy abundance.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Agriculture, manufacturing, sanitation, transportation, communications, computation, defense, and urban life all depend on the ability to convert energy into useful work.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Oil transformed geography and geopolitics. It created new corporations, altered military strategy, elevated some states, weakened others, and became inseparable from national security.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Every financial, political, and digital system remains grounded in the physical world.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Money coordinates claims on resources. Energy makes those resources useful.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">David Deutsch</h3><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">36. The Beginning of Infinity</h4><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Estimated reading time: 16–22 hours</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Deutsch examines explanation, criticism, fallibility, knowledge creation, and the conditions under which progress can continue.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Problems are inevitable. Solutions are not guaranteed, but they can continue to emerge wherever institutions permit conjecture, experimentation, criticism, and error correction.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Progress is neither automatic nor finite.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">It depends on a culture in which bad explanations can be challenged and better ones can replace them.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Yergin explains the capacity to act. Deutsch explains the capacity to discover. Energy without knowledge is brute force. Knowledge without energy remains unrealized potential.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Michael Saylor</h3><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">37. The Mobile Wave</h4><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Estimated reading time: 9–12 hours</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">I include my own book with some hesitation.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">It belongs here for a specific reason: it is an applied exercise in science, technology, and society.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Written in 2012, The Mobile Wave attempted to reason from first principles about what would happen when computing became mobile, software dematerialized products and services, and billions of people gained continuous access to networked intelligence.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The book examines how a general-purpose technology can reorganize education, commerce, media, payments, healthcare, transportation, employment, and the structure of enterprises.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Do not read it as an authority.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Read it as an auditable forecast.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Ask which predictions were correct, which were incomplete, which second-order consequences were missed, and which analytical methods proved useful.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Technological forecasting is not primarily about predicting a particular device. It is about identifying a new capability, understanding its economic advantages, and tracing what happens when that capability scales through a competitive society.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The larger lesson is that a digital transformation rarely preserves the existing institution and merely makes it faster. It frequently dematerializes the institution, redistributes power, changes its economics, and creates an entirely different system.</p><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">(<a href=\"https://books.apple.com/us/book/the-mobile-wave/id1534259034?utm_source=chatgpt.com\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">Apple</a>)</p><h2 style=\"font-size:1.35em;font-weight:600;margin:2.2em 0 0.7em 0;line-height:1.3;\">VIII. Sound Money and Bitcoin</h2><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Air, water, food, and energy sustain biological life.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Money coordinates economic life.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">A civilization needs clean money: a monetary system capable of preserving the economic energy generated by labor, ingenuity, and capital across time and space.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Corrupt the monetary system, and every price, contract, investment, and long-term calculation is affected.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Saifedean Ammous</h3><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">38. The Bitcoin Standard</h4><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">Estimated reading time: 10–13 hours</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The Bitcoin Standard places Bitcoin inside the history of monetary technologies.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">It examines why societies adopted shells, stones, metals, coins, gold, paper claims, government currency, and eventually digital money. It asks what properties allow a good to transmit value across time and space and what happens when a monetary system can be expanded or manipulated by privileged institutions.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The book then presents Bitcoin as digital hard money: scarce, global, decentralized, and governed by a protocol rather than the discretion of a political authority.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Its greatest contribution is the monetary framework.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Some of its broader cultural conclusions should be treated as arguments rather than universal laws, but its central question is indispensable:</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">What form of money best preserves individual choice, capital, and economic energy across generations?</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Read it after Rothbard, Yergin, Deutsch, and The Mobile Wave.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Rothbard explains money and political power.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Yergin explains energy.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Deutsch explains knowledge.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The Mobile Wave explains digital transformation.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The Bitcoin Standard brings those themes together around a monetary network.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Then read Satoshi Nakamoto’s original white paper. Commentary supplies context, but the engineer ultimately returns to the specification and the machine itself.</p><p style=\"margin:0.3em 0 1.3em 0;color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;font-style:italic;\">(<a href=\"https://www.wiley-vch.de/en/areas-interest/finance-economics-law/the-bitcoin-standard-978-1-119-47386-2?utm_source=chatgpt.com\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">Wiley-VCH</a>)</p><h2 style=\"font-size:1.35em;font-weight:600;margin:2.2em 0 0.7em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Read Adversarially</h2><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">These books should not be read for ideological confirmation.</p><ul style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Durant should be tested against modern scholarship.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Diamond should be balanced against human agency, institutions, and culture.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Keegan should be read alongside Clausewitz.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Livy should be distinguished from modern historiography.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Rothbard should be confronted with the strongest arguments for constitutional government and public authority.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Taleb’s skepticism should itself be subjected to skepticism.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Chernow’s protagonists should be studied rather than worshipped.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Yergin’s history should not be mistaken for a prediction that the future must resemble the past.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Deutsch’s optimism should be understood as conditional on institutions capable of criticism and correction.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">The Mobile Wave should be judged against the world that followed it.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">The Bitcoin Standard should be tested against the white paper, the code, the network, monetary history, and competing theories of money.</li></ul><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">No author should become a substitute for thought.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Read every work with three questions:</p><ol style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">What does this framework reveal that others miss?</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Where does it simplify reality too aggressively?</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">What decisions would change if it were correct?</li></ol><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The purpose of reading is not to memorize conclusions.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">It is to improve the ability to perceive reality, identify causality, recognize incentives, distinguish signal from noise, and act responsibly.</p><h2 style=\"font-size:1.35em;font-weight:600;margin:2.2em 0 0.7em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Counterweights and Primary Sources</h2><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Several additional works naturally extend the core curriculum.</p><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">On War, by Carl von Clausewitz</h4><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Read at least the major sections on the nature of war, political purpose, friction, uncertainty, and the relationship between defense and offense.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Clausewitz is the necessary counterweight to Keegan. A leader must understand both war’s rational strategic purpose and its tendency to escape rational control.</p><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">The Federalist Papers, by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay</h4><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">These essays present the strongest original arguments for the Constitution, federal power, institutional checks, representative government, and the management of faction.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">They are the natural counterweight to Rothbard’s account of the Constitution and the early federal government.</p><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Democracy in America, by Alexis de Tocqueville</h4><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Tocqueville examines democratic equality, civil society, religion, local government, individualism, majority power, associations, and administrative centralization.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">He explains both the productive strength of democratic society and the subtle pressures toward conformity and dependency.</p><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">What Has Government Done to Our Money?, by Murray Rothbard</h4><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This is the most accessible entry into Rothbard’s monetary thought.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">It introduces the development of money, inflation, banking, monetary competition, and government control over currency.</p><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">The Mystery of Banking, by Murray Rothbard</h4><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This provides a more detailed account of commercial banking, central banking, reserves, credit expansion, and monetary intervention.</p><h4 style=\"font-size:1.05em;font-weight:600;margin:1.6em 0 0.5em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System, by Satoshi Nakamoto</h4><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The white paper is not a substitute for understanding the functioning network, but it is the primary conceptual specification.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">A technological system should ultimately be studied through its original design, implementation, operation, and incentives, not merely through commentary about it.</p><h2 style=\"font-size:1.35em;font-weight:600;margin:2.2em 0 0.7em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Recommended Reading Sequence</h2><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">I would not read all eleven Durant volumes consecutively.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The curriculum will be more engaging and memorable if long narrative histories are alternated with analytical, philosophical, technological, and biographical works.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Phase One: Orientation</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Begin with:</p><ol style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">The Lessons of History</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Fooled by Randomness</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">The Black Swan</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">The Beginning of Infinity</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Guns, Germs, and Steel</li></ol><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">These works establish the central questions.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">What patterns recur across history?</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">How often do we confuse luck with skill?</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Why do extreme events dominate outcomes?</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">How do geography and inherited conditions shape possibility?</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Under what conditions can knowledge and progress continue?</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Phase Two: Foundations</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Proceed to:</p><ol style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Man, Economy, and State with Power and Market</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">The Ethics of Liberty</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Antifragile</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Skin in the Game</li></ol><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This phase establishes a theory of human action, a moral framework for liberty, an operational approach to uncertainty, and a doctrine of aligned incentives.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Phase Three: The Ancient World and War</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Read:</p><ol style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Durant Volumes I–IV</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Livy’s four surviving collections</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">A History of Warfare</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Selected portions of Clausewitz’s On War</li></ol><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The Durants provide scope.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Livy provides institutional depth and the Roman moral imagination.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Keegan supplies the anthropology and technology of warfare.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Clausewitz forces the reader to connect violence to political purpose.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Phase Four: Ideas and Liberty</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Read:</p><ol style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought, Volumes I and II</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Conceived in Liberty, Volumes I through V</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">The Federalist Papers</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Democracy in America</li></ol><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This phase connects economic ideas to political institutions and examines the continuing tension among liberty, order, federalism, democracy, local autonomy, and centralized power.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Phase Five: Capital, Energy, and Modernity</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Read:</p><ol style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Titan</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">The House of Morgan</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">The Prize</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Durant Volumes V–XI</li></ol><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This phase shows how commerce, banking, state finance, energy, information, industrial organization, and political power combined to create the modern world.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Phase Six: Digital Transformation and Sound Money</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Read:</p><ol style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">The Mobile Wave</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">The Bitcoin Standard</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">The Bitcoin white paper</li></ol><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This sequence moves from the digitization of information, products, services, and institutions to the digitization of property and money.</p><h3 style=\"font-size:1.25em;font-weight:600;margin:2em 0 0.6em 0;line-height:1.3;\">Phase Seven: Coda</h3><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Conclude with:</p><ol style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">The Bed of Procrustes</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">A second reading of The Lessons of History</li></ol><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Taleb’s aphorisms will carry more meaning after the reader has encountered centuries of institutional error, overconfidence, fragility, propaganda, and unintended consequences.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The Durants’ synthesis will also read differently. What initially appeared to be a set of general observations will have become a compressed index of recurring civilizational patterns. The underlying sequence remains consistent with the original curriculum’s movement from orientation through foundations, history, liberty, capital, energy, and final synthesis.</p><h2 style=\"font-size:1.35em;font-weight:600;margin:2.2em 0 0.7em 0;line-height:1.3;\">The Governing Idea</h2><ul style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">History without theory becomes anecdote.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Theory without history becomes ideology.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Technology without ethics becomes domination.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Rules that ignore incentives produce evasion, corruption, and failure.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Models without respect for uncertainty create fragility.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Capital without accountability becomes predation.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Power without limits becomes coercion.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Energy without knowledge is brute force.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Knowledge without energy remains potential.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Knowledge without liberty stagnates.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Liberty without order becomes chaos.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Order without liberty extinguishes initiative.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Money without integrity corrupts every long-term calculation.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\">Good intentions without competence produce unintended consequences.</li></ul><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The leaders of the future will operate machines of unprecedented scale: corporations, states, markets, energy grids, artificial intelligence systems, communication networks, and monetary protocols.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Their decisions will propagate farther and faster than those of any previous generation.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">They need more than intelligence.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">They need memory, judgment, humility, courage, discipline, and sound models.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">My mission is the digital transformation of energy, matter, property, capital, commerce, and trust.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Bitcoin is central to that project because it sits at the intersection of many of the forces studied in this curriculum: money and power, energy and information, property and trust, fixed rules and free markets, individual sovereignty and institutional authority.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">To understand Bitcoin fully, one must understand what it protects, what it replaces, what it consumes, what it coordinates, and which forms of power it constrains.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The natural allies in this mission are not merely technologists or investors.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">They are leaders who understand civilization well enough to preserve what works, reject what fails, and build what comes next.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Read to remember.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Read to reason.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\"><strong>Read to They want to keep validation accessible, protect node operators from unwanted costs and content, preserve affordable payments, and keep Bitcoin focused on sound money rather than general-purpose data storage. Those are serious concerns. I share the objectives. I disagree about the remedy.  <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0110.mediawiki\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">GitHub</a>)</span></p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This article critiques the proposal, not the people behind it. I assume good faith. Bitcoin is strongest when we can disagree vigorously without mistaking allies for enemies.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Nor is this a defense of every inscription, token, file, or application. Some may be frivolous, harmful, or fraudulent. The question is narrower: should a disputed use of currently valid, fee-paying transactions be addressed by changing consensus?</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Not every reason below carries equal weight, and several reinforce one another. The case is cumulative.</p><h2 style=\"font-size:1.35em;font-weight:600;margin:2.2em 0 0.7em 0;line-height:1.3;\">What BIP 110 Proposes</h2><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">This article addresses BIP 110 version 1.0.0, the \"Reduced Data Temporary Softfork,\" advanced to Complete on June 25, 2026. Under BIP 3, Complete means the authors have concluded their planned work and recommend adoption. It does not mean Bitcoin has adopted the proposal or that the community has reached consensus. The BIPs repository explicitly states that publication does not establish that a proposal is good, has community consensus, or is about to be adopted.  <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0110.mediawiki\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">GitHub</a>)</span></p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">During an approximately one-year active period, BIP 110 would add seven consensus restrictions. It would limit new scriptPubKeys to 34 bytes, with an 83-byte exception for OP_RETURN; limit many pushed payloads and script-argument witness items to 256 bytes; prohibit spending undefined witness and Tapleaf versions while still allowing such outputs to be created; prohibit the Taproot annex; cap Taproot control blocks at 257 bytes; reject Tapscripts containing OP_SUCCESSx opcodes; and reject Tapscript executions of OP_IF or OP_NOTIF.  <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0110.mediawiki\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">GitHub</a>)</span></p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The proposal grandfathers unspent transaction outputs created before activation. That is an important safeguard. I do not claim that BIP 110 broadly confiscates existing bitcoin. My objection is narrower: it prospectively removes currently valid transaction functionality, can affect rare pre-signed workflows that span activation, reduces technical optionality, and establishes a precedent for using consensus restrictions to discourage a category of otherwise valid use.  <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0110.mediawiki\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">GitHub</a>)</span></p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">BIP 110 also proposes a modified BIP 9 deployment. It uses a 55 percent miner-signaling threshold, compared with the 95 percent threshold specified in BIP 9; eliminates the conventional timeout and FAILED state; adds a mandatory-signaling period; guarantees lock-in on the enforcing chain no later than a specified height; and adds a new EXPIRED state after 52,416 active blocks.  <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0110.mediawiki\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">GitHub</a>)</span></p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">Like any soft fork, BIP 110 is not imposed by a central authority. Users choose which software and rules to enforce. The risk arises when economically significant participants enforce materially different rules, creating pressure, uncertainty, or a chain split.</p><p style=\"margin:0 0 1.15em 0;line-height:1.75;\">The authors provide a reference implementation, test vectors, a detailed rationale, and a candid discussion of tradeoffs. Those are substantive strengths of the document. The proposal argues that urgency and temporary duration justify the lower threshold and intentionally simple, blunt restrictions. I respect the concern and the work. I disagree with the risk calculus.  <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0110.mediawiki\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">GitHub</a>)</span></p><h2 style=\"font-size:1.35em;font-weight:600;margin:2.2em 0 0.7em 0;line-height:1.3;\">I. Neutrality and First Principles</h2><ol style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Consensus is Bitcoin’s most powerful intervention.</strong> A soft fork makes some blocks that were valid under prior rules invalid to upgraded nodes. That power should be reserved for clear, serious, and broadly understood failures.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>It is not a repair for an established consensus failure.</strong> BIP 110 does not correct inflation, signature validation, double spending, or a known critical bug. It addresses a contested externality and use case, so the burden of proof should be especially high.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>It elevates a contested judgment into protocol law.</strong> The proposal moves a dispute about legitimate use and externalities from relay policy, mining policy, and markets into consensus validity.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Bitcoin cannot read intent.</strong> The network cannot know whether bytes represent an image, a proof, a contract, metadata, an authentication record, or a future application.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Structural proxies create collateral risk.</strong> Because intent cannot be known, the proposal restricts technical forms that may serve both disfavored and legitimate purposes.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>A social message is not sufficient grounds for a consensus change.</strong> The specification expressly treats activation as a way to communicate that data storage is unwelcome. Consensus should be changed for compelling technical or monetary reasons, not primarily to express disapproval.  <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0110.mediawiki\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">GitHub</a>)</span></li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Disapproval is not invalidity.</strong> A transaction can be trivial, speculative, offensive, or wasteful and still follow the rules and pay the fee required for inclusion.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>It narrows prospective economic freedom on the BIP 110 chain.</strong> Pre-activation UTXOs are grandfathered, but users creating UTXOs during the active period would have fewer valid ways to structure and spend them than under existing consensus.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Permissionless systems must tolerate unapproved experimentation.</strong> Requiring innovators to prove their use worthy before building reverses the meaning of permissionless innovation.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>It turns protocol conservatism upside down.</strong> Conservatism at the base layer should mean reluctance to alter consensus, not eagerness to alter consensus in favor of a conservative use philosophy.</li></ol><h2 style=\"font-size:1.35em;font-weight:600;margin:2.2em 0 0.7em 0;line-height:1.3;\">II. The Burden of Proof Has Not Been Met</h2><ol start=\"11\" style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>\"Spam\" is not a consensus primitive.</strong> There is no opcode that can distinguish spam from utility. Those labels arise from human judgment.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>\"Monetary\" and \"nonmonetary\" are not cleanly separable.</strong> A payment channel, proof of reserves, custody policy, smart contract, or settlement commitment is both financial activity and data.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Known use cases are not the full design space.</strong> The proposal says it preserves all known monetary use cases. Innovation is defined by what is not yet known.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>The BIP itself does not quantify the node burden it would remove.</strong> It describes costs but does not estimate the relevant bandwidth, storage, validation load, hardware thresholds, or number of node operators likely to be gained or lost.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>It does not quantify the decentralization benefit.</strong> The claim that BIP 110 would improve decentralization is not paired with a measurable model or target.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>It does not quantify payment relief.</strong> It does not estimate how much transaction fees would fall, for how long, or how many payment users would benefit.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>It combines distinct costs into one diagnosis.</strong> UTXO-state growth, initial-sync bandwidth, archival storage, relay burden, and validation time have different causes and may require different remedies.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Urgency is asserted rather than operationally defined.</strong> The proposal calls the situation urgent and a crisis, but provides no objective threshold at which consensus intervention becomes necessary.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>A historical relay-policy limit is not proof of an optimal consensus limit.</strong> An 83-byte default may be useful policy without becoming a timeless block-validity rule.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>The 256-byte line is heuristic.</strong> The rationale relates it partly to compressed image size and large cryptographic integers, but does not establish 256 bytes as an optimal boundary between safety and innovation.  <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0110.mediawiki\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">GitHub</a>)</span></li></ol><h2 style=\"font-size:1.35em;font-weight:600;margin:2.2em 0 0.7em 0;line-height:1.3;\">III. The Technical Scope Is Too Broad</h2><ol start=\"21\" style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Seven separate consensus changes are bundled together.</strong> Participants cannot support one restriction and reject another. They must accept or reject the package.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>The strongest technical concern is bundled with unrelated restrictions.</strong> Large scriptPubKeys can increase UTXO-state and validation costs. If that creates a measurable hazard, it deserves a narrowly scoped proposal on its own, not automatic support for six additional restrictions.  <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0110.mediawiki\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">GitHub</a>)</span></li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>The 83-byte OP_RETURN policy becomes consensus.</strong> That converts a configurable relay and mining preference into a block-validity rule.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>The 256-byte limits constrain general primitives.</strong> They target data storage by restricting broad classes of pushed payloads and script-argument witness items.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Spending undefined witness and Tapleaf versions would be disabled.</strong> Those spaces are unused today in part because they are reserved for future upgrades.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>The Taproot annex would be disabled.</strong> BIP 341 reserves the annex for future extensions. Even if users should not employ it before its meaning is defined, closing a deliberate upgrade path should require exceptional justification.  <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0341.mediawiki\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">GitHub</a>)</span></li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Taptree depth would be reduced.</strong> A 257-byte control-block cap limits revealed script paths to seven levels and can constrain complex script trees.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>OP_SUCCESSx would be disabled even in unexecuted branches.</strong> BIP 342 created these opcodes as clean upgrade hooks for future soft forks.  <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0342.mediawiki\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">GitHub</a>)</span></li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Executed OP_IF and OP_NOTIF would be prohibited in Tapscript.</strong> The authors regard them as redundant and commonly abused, but also acknowledge experimental uses and possible Miniscript efficiencies.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>The proposal openly accepts bluntness in exchange for speed.</strong> Its rationale says a better-balanced approach would require more development and review, so it chooses simpler restrictions intended for faster deployment. Urgency is not a substitute for precision in consensus code.  <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0110.mediawiki\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">GitHub</a>)</span></li></ol><h2 style=\"font-size:1.35em;font-weight:600;margin:2.2em 0 0.7em 0;line-height:1.3;\">IV. upgrade paths at once.</strong> Annexes, future witness versions, future Tapleaf versions, and OP_SUCCESSx are all part of Bitcoin’s reserved design space.  <span style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">GitHub</a>)</span></li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Reserved does not mean useless.</strong> It means earlier designers deliberately preserved option value for needs that had not yet emerged.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>A one-year closure can still disrupt development timelines.</strong> The authors expect future soft forks to require more than a year of coordination, but that is an estimate, not a guarantee.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>It may complicate BitVM-style designs.</strong> The creates a narrow but admitted fund-access risk.</strong> The BIP candidly identifies rare pre-signed Taproot scenarios in which post-activation UTXOs could be frozen or spent unexpectedly.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Grandfathering is valuable but not complete insulation.</strong> Pre-activation UTXOs are protected, yet workflows that create or spend affected outputs during the deployment can still encounter new constraints.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Users are advised to migrate potentially affected funds.</strong> A proposal that requires even a narrow class of users to migrate is not a costless filter.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>\"No known use case\" is not a safety proof.</strong> Private systems, unpublished contracts, experimental wallets, and future protocols are not fully observable.  <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0110.mediawiki\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">GitHub</a>)</span></li></ol><h2 style=\"font-size:1.35em;font-weight:600;margin:2.2em 0 0.7em 0;line-height:1.3;\">V. style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Grandfathering makes validity history-dependent.</strong> The same spending construction can be treated differently depending on when the UTXO was created.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>History-dependent rules increase implementation complexity.</strong> Every implementation must identify the relevant UTXO creation height and style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>It removes the conventional FAILED outcome.</strong> The proposed deployment cannot simply time out in the ordinary BIP 9 manner.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>It creates several coordination windows.</strong> Voluntary signaling, mandatory signaling, lock-in, activation, and expiration each introduce opportunities for 0;line-height:1.3;\">VI. The Economic and Security Effects Are Uncertain</h2><ol start=\"51\" style=\"margin:0 0 1.3em 0;padding-left:1.4em;line-height:1.75;\"><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>The node externality is real but heterogeneous.</strong> Every fully validating node must download and verify blocks, while pruned nodes can discard old raw block data and limit historical storage. The relevant costs should be measured separately.  <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://bitcoincore.org/en/releases/0.11.0/?utm_source=chatgpt.com\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">Bitcoin Core</a>)</span></li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>The fee-recipient issue is not unique to data transactions.</strong> Miners collect fees while validators bear some costs for every transaction. The magnitude may differ, but the basic structure is universal.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Technical costs should be measured directly.</strong> For a given amount of data and validation work, resource costs arise from bytes, state, computation, and bandwidth, not from whether observers approve of the transaction’s purpose.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>BIP 110 cannot eliminate data embedding.</strong> The specification acknowledges that users can split data into smaller pieces or disguise it within permitted structures.  <span style=\"color:#8a8a8a;font-size:0.92em;\">(<a href=\"https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0110.mediawiki\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">GitHub</a>)</span></li><li the underlying demand.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>The fee effect is ambiguous.</strong> Suppressing one use may lower payment fees, reduce aggregate fee revenue, shift demand into href=\"https://developer.bitcoin.org/reference/block_chain.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com\" style=\"color:inherit;text-decoration:underline;\">Bitcoin Developer Docs</a>)</span></li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Lower aggregate fee demand can weaken security at the margin.</strong> To the extent BIP 110 reduces total fee demand rather than merely reallocating it, lower channels, custody systems, financial applications, and other uses need not peak at the same time.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>The specification does not model the security style=\"font-size:1.35em;font-weight:600;margin:2.2em 0 0.7em 0;line-height:1.3;\">VII. privileges incumbent use cases.</strong> \"All known monetary use cases\" protects the present, not the future.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>It destroys option value before value can style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Future Layer 2 systems may depend on today’s unused hooks.</strong> Base-layer optionality can support scale without requiring frequent base-layer activity.</li><li style=\"margin-bottom:0.4em;\"><strong>Applications can strengthen money.</strong> Better wallets, custody, settlement, credit, securities, and proof systems can increase Bitcoin’s
